title: Migration
objective: After this level you can explain how birds migrate thousands of miles.
summary: In 2022 a young godwit flew about 13,560 km nonstop on stored fat. Tracked Arctic terns fly about 70,900 km a year. Migrants steer by the sun, the stars and magnetism.

cards.headline: A young bird flew for 11 days without landing once.
cards.body: In October 2022, a juvenile bar-tailed godwit tagged B6 left Alaska and flew nonstop across the Pacific to Tasmania, Australia. No stops for food, water or rest. How does any bird pull that off?

cards.fact: About 13,560 km in one go: the longest nonstop flight on record.
cards.context: That's 8,425 miles, tracked by a 5-gram solar-powered satellite tag. The U.S. Geological Survey calls it the longest documented nonstop flight by any animal. The fuel was fat: B6 fattened up on Alaska's Kuskokwim Delta before leaving, and some migrating birds double their body weight before a journey. The fuel tank is the bird.

mascot.line: You don't need the kilometers. Remember the fuel: fat, stored before takeoff.

cards.headline: The tern that follows summer
cards.body: The Arctic tern goes farther, just not in one hop. In a 2010 study, scientists fitted 11 terns from Greenland and Iceland with 1.4-gram geolocators. On average, each flew 70,900 km a year between the Arctic and the Southern Ocean, with a stopover in the North Atlantic: the longest round-trip migration ever recorded electronically. In 2016, Newcastle University reported a Farne Islands tern with an estimated 96,000 km round trip.

cards.fact: A tern's lifetime of flying could take it to the Moon and back three times.
cards.context: Arctic terns can live more than 30 years, so the 2010 study estimated a lifetime of migrations may top 2.4 million km. And they don't get lost: migrating birds can tell which direction they're flying from the sun, the stars and Earth's magnetic field. Sun, stars and magnetism: three compasses in one small head.

cards.headline: Migration: explained

questions.prompt: About how far did the bar-tailed godwit B6 fly nonstop in 2022?

options.label: About 70,900 km
options.rationale: That's an Arctic tern's average yearly total.

questions.explanation: B6 flew about 13,560 km (8,425 miles) from Alaska to Tasmania in 11 days without landing.

questions.prompt: How could B6 fly for 11 days without stopping to eat?

options.label: It caught insects in the air
options.rationale: It made no stops for food at all.

options.label: It slept on the waves each night
It slowed into torpor to save fuel
It burned fat stored before takeoff

questions.explanation: B6 fattened up on Alaska's Kuskokwim Delta, then ran on that stored fat the whole way.

questions.prompt: An Arctic tern flies farther each year than B6's record flight. Why does the godwit still hold the nonstop record?

options.label: The tern's route is shorter than it looks
options.rationale: Tracked terns averaged 70,900 km a year.

options.label: The godwit flew higher than the tern
options.rationale: The record is about distance without stopping.

options.label: The tern migrates only every other year
options.rationale: The 70,900 km is a yearly figure.

questions.explanation: The tern's huge yearly trip includes stopovers; B6 covered its 13,560 km without landing once.
